title: OOP in R: #1 Intro
text:
Welcome back to another entry in this blog!
Starting today, I will work on a short series of blog posts on object-oriented programming (OOP) in R. While R itself is a so-called functional programming language, which evolves around defining and chaining functions, it also contains capabilities for OOP. And everyone has come across this neat feature in R, even if without knowing it. OOP in R is for example responsible for why plot() works differently for different types of input, or why we can often just call predict() to generate predictions or forecasts based on a fitted model, (mostly) regardless of the method used for generating the fitted model.
To illustrate the behavior of plot():

set.seed(1)        # starting point for random number generation
x <- rnorm(10)     # just a standard vector
x_ts <- ts(x)      # an object of class "ts"

# Create plots
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), cex = 1)
plot(x)
plot(x_ts)







Figure 1: Example plots for different input objects. Left is a scatter plot, right is a line plot.





When applying plot(x), where x is just a numeric vector, we obtain a scatter plot, where R uses the values of x on the \(y\)-axis. On the contrary, when we apply plot() to an object of class "ts", here to x_ts, which we have created using ts(), the plotting function returns a line plot. Therefore, R can apparently distinguish between different entities and make the same function behave quite differently. During this series, we will investigate, how this behavior arises.
Furthermore, we will consider a very particular example to create our own object class using three different OOP systems in R. In detail, we create a system to better deal with so-called spatial time series. For this purpose, we will use one-minute closing prices of the S&P 500 from September 01, 2026, to September 18, 2026, which are available in my GitHub repository called datasets.

url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dschulz13/datasets/refs/heads/main/One-minute%20closing%20prices_%5EGSPC_2026-09-01_to_2026-09-20.csv"
dataset <- read.csv(url, check.names = FALSE)
head(dataset, 3)

      Time 2026-09-01 2026-09-02 2026-09-03 2026-09-04 2026-09-08 2026-09-09
1 09:30:00    7629.01    7638.29    7702.06    7736.69    7709.89    7653.67
2 09:31:00    7633.35    7634.67    7701.22    7741.47    7705.91    7651.97
3 09:32:00    7634.28    7640.29    7702.51    7743.00    7704.01    7648.35
  2026-09-10 2026-09-11 2026-09-14 2026-09-15 2026-09-16 2026-09-17 2026-09-18
1    7593.82    7657.91    7597.94    7614.18    7606.13    7641.14    7642.94
2    7592.97    7656.83    7598.48    7604.34    7604.33    7632.16    7647.89
3    7592.08    7661.95    7600.87    7605.97    7603.52    7634.31    7646.34


Especially the plotting of spatial time series can be tedious, as it involves creating 3D figures using libraries such as plotly.

library(plotly)
library(lubridate)
library(dplyr)

dims <- dim(dataset[, -1])

# Matrix with decimal time points
decimal_time <- dataset %>%
  pull(Time) %>%
  hms() %>%
  as.numeric() %>%
  `/`(., 3600) %>%
  rep(dims[[2]]) %>%
  matrix(nrow = dims[[1]], ncol = dims[[2]])

# Matrix with decimal dates
decimal_year <- names(dataset)[-1] %>%
  as.Date() %>%
  decimal_date() %>%
  rep(dims[[1]]) %>%
  matrix(nrow = dims[[1]], ncol = dims[[2]], byrow = TRUE)

# Matrix with closing prices
close <- dataset[, -1] %>%
  unname() %>%
  as.matrix()

# Plot creation
plot_ly(x = decimal_year, y = decimal_time, z = close, type = "surface",
        showscale = FALSE) %>%
  layout(
    scene = list(
      xaxis = list(autorange = "reversed", title = "Decimal year"),
      yaxis = list(autorange = "reversed", title = "Time of day"),
      zaxis = list(title = "Closing price")
    )
  )







Figure 2: A 3D plot of a spatial time series. Readers can also interact with it.




Figure 2 is then a first draft of a plot of a spatial time series that still has a few formatting issues. In a time consuming manner, we need to create matrices for all \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\) coordinates. For better formatting, for example of the decimal year tick labels, we would need to implement further plotly functions. And thus, such a code can easily become quite convoluted. This motivates the development of an object class "spts" (spatial time series), which only contains the observed values and the time points of the two time axes, and to which we may then easily apply predefined standard functions, such as for plotting. This will strongly simplify the workflow in such contexts.
In the next post, we will therefore start implementing such an idea using the S3 system, the simplest OOP system in R. Stay tuned for more!
Best,Dominik

(Version: September 22, 2026)

title: Welcome to Stats Rsenal
text:
Welcome to Stats Rsenal!
Starting a blog on data analysis with a focus on programming has been a long-time idea of mine. However, due to other obligations the realization was postponed time and time again. Nonetheless, now it is finally time to start this project and bring the joy of data analysis to the world.
On an irregular basis, I will share with you posts teaching about programming, applied statistics, machine learning, and time series analysis.
Please feel free to learn more about me on my homepage, and reach out, if you have feedback on my posts.
Stay tuned for exciting updates! With that being said, what better way is there to start such a blog than with the most popular words in the world of programming?

title: Hi everyone, I’m Dr. Dominik Schulz!
text:
I am a former PhD student and a former scientific employee at the Chair of Econometrics and Quantitative Methods, Faculty of Business Administration and Economics, Paderborn University. My training includes statistics and data science and the focus of my research so far is on time series analysis as well as the development of statistical software in this context, in particular for the free software R. Nonetheless, I am also versatile in MySQL and Python, which I appreciate more and more in my own workflows.



Statistician & Data Scientist






This site functions both as a personal website and a blog (called Stats Rsenal) on topics related to data science, time series analysis, and programming. However, new blog posts will only appear irregularly. Regarding programming topics, I will mainly focus on R but also incorporate posts on SQL or Python from time to time.


If you have any feedback or suggestions, please feel free to reach out via dominik.schulz.r@gmail.com.
